Q: How to remove special characters in a file name (\u202a, \u202c, \u200f) when renaming with Python A:

The folowing retains only ASCII characters:

"".join([char for char in filename if ord(char) < 128])
#'My Song.mp3'

Q: How to create a comprehension where items are lambda functions with a single argument? A:

Use a function to create each lambda:

def make_fn(i):
    return lambda e: e[i]

e0, e1, e2 = [make_fn(i) for i in range(3)]

Now:

t = 'abc'
print(e0(t), e1(t), e2(t)) # a b c

And this will correctly fail:

e0(t, 2)
# TypeError: <lambda>() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

Q: Seeking Roadmap and Advanced Resources for Deepening JavaScript Knowledge A:

There is no way around it, you really need to be/get comfortable - in terms of not even thinking of them anymore as such, but you breathe it/them - with the core features of the language, which are ...

  • functions and closures ... they are both everywhere.

  • delegation - both of its kinds ...

    • the implicit, prototype-based, automatic delegation mechanism, hence inheritance.

    • explicit delegation via `call` and `apply` and their "lazy" cousin `bind`.

  • `async`/`await` and `Promise`s ... do not skip them.

At the same time, you need to accept that class-based inheritance is neither a synonym for, nor does it equal the concept of OOP; it never was/did. OOP is about objects, how they encapsulate data and how they communicate - no classes needed.

Nevertheless, I would encourage every novice to choose class-syntax when it comes to implementing own types where one needs more than just one object of the same shape at a given time. Class syntax is not just, as it so often gets (mis)quoted ... "syntactical sugar over prototypes". It reaches beyond that, and it enables/ensures well-structured code-bases and optimized engine-handling/execution.

But in order to "breathe"/"inhale" the language to its fullest, right from the beginning, I suggest two research projects that both target composition; one for object-composition and the other one for function-composition.

You could e.g. try to tackle the domain of object-composition by implementing a function-based mixin that mimics JavaScript's `EventTarget` type (which forces you into a deep-dive into event-systems). And as for the "functional" aspect, I suggest you implement at least one of the two behaviors which both are capable of altering the timing of a function's execution, while said function actually is called repeatedly. Choose either `throttle` or `debounce`, and build it in the form of a function that accepts a function-type parameter along with (an) additional timing parameter/s, and which returns another function that controls the invocation of its consumed function (the one that was passed as argument).

In case that is too much for the beginning, get comfortable first mostly with `Array` methods (of the prototype kind) and with all the static `Object` methods that enable you to build exactly (or close to) the kind of type-systems one preferably does build via class-constructors.

Have a closer look at `WeakMap`s and `WeakSet`s, as well as at `Map` and `Set`. If you are curious enough, make a detour to `Proxy`/ies.

And always remember, `function` is your mightiest tool, for it implements behavior and expresses intent. It's your closest/most valued ally, next to modules and plain objects — where modules are for grouping/managing domain-specific implementations, and plain objects are for grouping/managing pure data.

Q: Nested query in POwerQuery A:

It's way more performant to group the data by SessionID in the first place

let
    Source = Table1,
    #"Grouped Table" = Table.Group(Source, "SessionID", {"grp", each if List.Contains([SessionContent], "Some Data I don't want", (x,y) => Text.Contains(x,y, Comparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) then null else _}),
    #"Expanded grp" = Table.ExpandTableColumn(Table.SelectRows(#"Grouped Table", each not ([grp] is null)), "grp", {"SequenceNumber", "SessionContent"})
in
    #"Expanded grp"

Q: Why can't I use Spotify's Web API for free anymore? A:

"Why can't I use Spotify's Web API for free anymore?"

Because they changed it.

According this Spotify Blog post:

"Over time, advances in automation and AI have fundamentally altered the usage patterns and risk profile of developer access, and at Spotify's current scale these risks now require more structured controls.

In response, we are making changes to Spotify for Developers to better protect creators, partners, listeners and the platform."

That's what >they< say. Anything else would be speculation / conjecture ... and opinion.

"... why do the videos and tutorials I see (like this video) use the API without premium?".

Because they are out of date! They may have been correct before, but not anymore.

"People are going to use my program, and not everyone has premium."

That's too bad. I guess that it means that those people who don't have Spotify Premium won't be able to use your program.

If you write a program that depends on a free API and that API becomes non-free, you are screwed. You should consider that possibility before writing the program.

Remember:

  • "There Ain't No Such Thing As A Free Lunch."
  • "If the service is free, you are the product."

By the way, if you attempted to work around these (new) Spotify restrictions, you (or the people using your program) would probably be violating the Spotify terms of service. There could be consequences for doing that.
